subtitle: Give new colleagues a start that is easy to understand and accessible. This course helps you connect each new employee with the work, the people and the support they need.
scope: For DHS supervisors and team leaders welcoming new employees. These planning activities supplement actual agency onboarding, required training, authorized access, and HR procedures. They do not change probation, employment terms, accommodation processes, or training-credit rules. Use practice information in course exercises.
introTranscript: A welcome message matters, but an inclusive start requires more than friendliness. A new colleague needs to understand the work, find useful information, contribute without guessing unwritten expectations, and ask for support without being treated as a problem. This course follows the first weeks of employment through preparation, access, explanation, relationships, early work and follow-through. You will build a usable plan rather than a longer information packet. Supervisors remain responsible for their work; the Equity and Inclusion Operations Consultant offers guidance and feedback. The examples are practice and the timing suggestions are planning choices, not agency deadlines.

lessons.title: Prepare a start someone can actually use
lessons.summary: Plan the first days around understandable actions rather than the amount of information delivered.
lessons.objective: Identify the information a new employee needs before arriving and during the first day.
objectives: Identify the information a new employee needs before arriving and during the first day.
Assign an owner and confirmation step to a necessary preparation task.
Separate required agency onboarding from optional relationship-building activities.
takeaways: A welcoming start needs usable arrangements.
Name who owns each preparation task.
Explain what is required and what is optional.
lessons.statement: Read the first-day plan from the perspective of someone who does not yet know how this workplace works.

image.caption: Preparation removes avoidable confusion before a colleague arrives.

intro.heading: Begin before the welcome meeting
intro.body:
A new employee can receive a polished welcome email and still arrive without the access, directions or schedule needed to begin. A supervisor may assume that another office has arranged equipment or that an employee already knows which entrance to use. These small gaps can make the first day feel like a test of resourcefulness rather than an introduction to the work. Preparing a usable start means asking what the person must do, what they need to do it, and who will confirm that it is ready.

Divide preparation into a few decisions. What must the employee know before arrival? What should happen on the first day? What can wait until the employee has enough context to understand it? Directions, a named contact, the start arrangement and a short schedule are often more useful beforehand than a large folder of background material. Use current agency instructions for actual employment documents and required activities; this learning plan is not a substitute.

Assign ownership instead of relying on the word “handled.” If equipment is expected, identify the person who confirms availability and the fallback if it is delayed. If the employee will work remotely, explain how to join the first contact and how to reach someone when the connection fails. Do not share passwords, grant unauthorized access, or bypass normal approvals in the name of making a start convenient.

An inclusive plan also distinguishes invitation from obligation. A team social event, voluntary learning resource or optional community should not sound like a condition of belonging. Explain the purpose and offer a reasonable alternative way to make connections. Do not require a personal story, cultural disclosure or identity explanation as an icebreaker.

Finally, check the plan with a colleague unfamiliar with its details. Can they identify the next action, the contact and the expected result? Where do they have to guess? A brief test can reveal assumptions the supervisor no longer notices.

lessons.keyStatement: A preparation task is not complete until the person can use its result.

flashcards.back: The continuing process of helping a new colleague understand, access and contribute to the workplace.
An introduction to agency information and requirements within the wider onboarding process.
The role responsible for confirming that an arrangement is ready or resolving its delay.
A workplace habit treated as obvious even though it has not been explained.
An opportunity someone may decline without losing access to work or fair treatment.

items.title: A long welcome attachment
items.body: A packet can preserve useful detail while still obscuring immediate actions. Put the first contact, practical arrangements and short schedule where the employee can find them. Introduce the remaining material when it becomes relevant. Keep current required instructions intact and explain their purpose rather than replacing them with an informal summary.

items.title: An unconfirmed access request
items.body: A submitted request is evidence of activity, not evidence that access works. Ask the responsible role to confirm the result. Plan an appropriate task the employee can begin if access is delayed, and a contact for resolution. Do not turn the delay into an unfavorable judgment about the employee.

items.title: An informal team tradition
items.body: A tradition may feel friendly to insiders and obligatory to newcomers. Explain that participation is optional when it is optional, avoid requiring personal disclosure, and offer another way to connect. Belonging should be demonstrated in ordinary work interactions, not measured by participation in one social event.

tabs.label: Action
tabs.body: An action tells the new employee what they can actually do. “Complete the usual setup” assumes experience they do not yet have. A named destination, useful instruction and first task reduce guessing. Confirm the action works before relying on it: a submitted request is preparation activity, while a usable approved account is a readiness result.

tabs.label: Owner
tabs.body: An owner identifies who confirms or repairs the arrangement. A long list of possible contacts can leave a newcomer unsure where to begin. Name a practical first contact and explain when another role must decide. This keeps responsibility with the people who can resolve the issue rather than testing whether a new colleague can navigate informal networks.

tabs.label: Fallback
tabs.body: A fallback provides a legitimate next action when preparation is delayed. The employee might use approved training material while IT resolves access, with clear follow-up from the supervisor. Borrowing someone else’s account is not a workable shortcut: it changes security and accountability. Preserve progress through approved alternatives, and keep the unresolved dependency visible.

check.question: A supervisor has submitted equipment and access requests but has not checked the results. What should happen before the employee starts?
check.correct: Confirm readiness with the responsible roles and provide a clear fallback and contact for any unresolved arrangement.
wrong: Mark preparation complete because every request was submitted.
Give the employee a colleague’s account to avoid delay.
Ask the employee to sort out the arrangements alone as a sign of initiative.
check.feedbackCorrect: Preparation includes a usable result and a response when something is delayed. It also preserves approved access procedures.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A request record shows action was started, not that equipment and access are ready. A colleague’s account bypasses approved access and obscures responsibility. Asking the newcomer to solve the whole gap alone transfers a preventable setup problem. Confirm results with responsible roles and provide an approved fallback with a clear owner.

items.text: The named contact and first-day joining instructions.
A detailed explanation of a later quarterly planning process.
An invitation to a voluntary social gathering.
Whether the required account is ready to use.
Background reading for a project not yet assigned.
A voluntary employee community with a clear purpose.

lessons.next: Next, examine whether the materials and support are accessible.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Malik will start in a hybrid policy role. Supervisor Ellen has sent twenty attachments and written “see you Monday.” Equipment is delayed, and the team’s morning coffee gathering appears on the schedule without explanation. Malik has not received joining directions.
scenario.prompt: Which revision provides the clearest start?
options: Send another attachment telling Malik to be flexible.
Make coffee attendance mandatory so Malik meets everyone.
Send brief joining instructions, confirm owners and fallbacks for equipment, and explain the optional gathering separately.
responses: More information will not resolve the missing arrangements. Malik still has to guess how to begin.
A social invitation should not become a condition of belonging or a substitute for a practical start.
This makes the first actions usable, assigns responsibility and distinguishes a voluntary connection from required work.

lessons.transfer: Using a practice newcomer, rewrite the first-day message in six clear sentences. Include joining information, a contact, required actions, optional invitations and an unresolved-task fallback.

move.control: You can confirm arrangements, explain priorities and name the appropriate contact without bypassing approved processes.
move.failure: The welcome looks complete, but the employee cannot begin without guessing or borrowing another person’s access.
move.next: Before the next start date, review the first-day plan with a colleague who did not prepare it.

lessons.title: Make access and support easy to request
lessons.summary: Offer clear ways to address barriers without asking the new colleague to disclose private information to the team.
lessons.objective: Identify a barrier in a common onboarding material or meeting.
objectives: Identify a barrier in a common onboarding material or meeting.
Write a neutral offer of support that does not presume an employee’s disability or identity.
Route an accommodation request through the responsible agency process.
takeaways: Ask about the arrangement, not a diagnosis.
Formal requests follow responsible agency processes.
lessons.statement: A person should not have to explain their private history to find a usable way to begin.

image.caption: Materials and meeting arrangements should be usable before someone has to ask for a workaround.

intro.heading: Provide a clear route without an identity test
intro.body:
Onboarding often includes documents, online forms, meetings and demonstrations. A barrier in any one of them can delay participation. A scanned document may be difficult to navigate, a fast demonstration may leave no way to review the steps, and a meeting invitation may omit a useful agenda. These are features of the arrangement to examine. They are not evidence that the new employee is unprepared or that the supervisor needs a personal diagnosis.

Start with materials designed for understandable use. Organize headings, explain unfamiliar abbreviations, provide meaningful links and use the agency’s accessibility guidance. Offer a written follow-up to a complex demonstration. Tell the employee which contact handles access problems, questions and accommodation requests. A generic promise that “our door is always open” is less useful when the person does not know which door or how to begin.

A neutral support question can focus on the activity: “Are the materials and joining arrangements working for you? Here is the contact if a different arrangement is needed.” This does not require everyone to disclose personal information. Some issues are ordinary usability improvements the supervisor can make for the whole group; others require the formal accommodation process. Do not promise an accommodation decision, demand medical information in a learning activity, or dismiss a request because the employee appears to manage another task.

Keep private information within the approved process. The team may need to know how to conduct a meeting or share a document, but it generally does not need a colleague’s personal explanation. Seek the responsible office’s guidance on what is appropriate to communicate. Course notes should use invented details, never real medical records or an employee’s request history.

After an arrangement changes, check whether it works for the intended activity. The existence of a file, caption setting or device does not by itself establish usable access. A practical check asks whether the colleague can obtain the information and take part without unnecessary obstacles.

lessons.keyStatement: Address the participation barrier without making private disclosure the price of access.

items.title: The document is difficult to use
items.body: Check the document’s structure and the approved accessible alternative. Do not simply ask the employee to find someone to read it aloud. Confirm that the revised material communicates the needed information. An improvement for one colleague may also make the document easier for others to navigate.

items.title: The employee asks for a different arrangement
items.body: Listen to the request and explain the responsible agency contact and process. Avoid making an immediate legal determination or asking the team to vote on the request. The supervisor’s helpful response includes timely routing, practical communication and following the approved decision, not independent diagnosis.

items.title: A colleague asks why support is provided
items.body: Explain the team’s participation arrangements without revealing private information. People may use different supports to do the work. Questions about official requirements belong with the responsible office. Do not make the newcomer defend their need publicly as a condition of receiving ordinary respectful treatment.

tabs.label: Clear materials
tabs.body: Clear materials make the ordinary path easier to use: meaningful headings, accurate instructions and a clear contact help people act without revealing personal circumstances. A simplified welcome document may remove confusion, but it cannot establish that every person can use it. Check the actual task and offer an appropriate route when a remaining barrier is identified.

tabs.label: Formal requests
tabs.body: A formal support request follows the agency’s responsible process, including appropriate information handling. The supervisor should not make the person present a medical history to the team or wait for a special phrase before responding. Explain who handles the request and promptly forward it as required, preserving the distinction between practical document improvement and an authorized accommodation decision.

tabs.label: Practical check
tabs.body: The practical check asks whether the arrangement enables the intended participation. Sending a different file is an activity, not evidence that it can be read or used. Confirm usability with the employee without unnecessary personal inquiry. If the barrier remains, return to the responsible role; do not interpret an inaccessible orientation exercise as unwillingness to learn.

check.question: A new employee says the orientation document is unusable with their reading setup. What is the strongest response?
check.correct: Address the document barrier, explain the responsible support route if needed, and confirm that the revised arrangement is usable.
wrong: Ask the employee to describe their medical history to the team.
Treat the complaint as reluctance to learn the material.
Assume that sending any alternate file completes the issue.
check.feedbackCorrect: The response focuses on participation and appropriate support, with a check of the result.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Medical disclosure to the whole team is not needed to fix the document barrier. Calling the concern reluctance replaces an access question with a motive assumption. Any alternate file may still be unusable. Address the actual participation need, follow the responsible support process and check whether the arrangement works.

items.text: Add clear headings to a confusing orientation handout.
Explain the designated agency route for an accommodation request.
Ask the employee to justify a diagnosis during team introductions.
Provide a written summary of a complex demonstration.
Seek approved guidance about an individualized support request.
Include medical information in a shared onboarding tracker.

lessons.next: Next, explain the work and its unwritten expectations.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Asha cannot navigate the scanned orientation packet efficiently. Supervisor Devon offers to announce Asha’s access needs at the team meeting. Asha only asked for a usable version of the packet. The team has no need for personal details.
options: Arrange a usable packet and explain the support route privately if needed, without disclosing personal information to the team.
Announce the request so colleagues understand why Asha needs assistance.
Wait for Asha to solve the problem because the same packet worked for others.
responses: This addresses the barrier while respecting the responsible process and the employee’s privacy.
The team needs workable arrangements, not private information that Asha did not ask to share.
Past use by others does not establish usability for the current task or person.

lessons.transfer: Review one practice onboarding document and one meeting invitation. List the barrier, a general improvement, the responsible contact and a result check.

move.control: You can make instructions clearer, route requests promptly and communicate approved arrangements appropriately.
move.failure: The team receives personal information while the actual access barrier remains unresolved.
move.next: Add a clear, neutral support route to the next onboarding message and test the essential materials.

lessons.title: Explain the work without making people guess
lessons.summary: Translate team shorthand and expectations into specific examples a new colleague can use.
lessons.objective: Rewrite an unwritten expectation as an observable work agreement.
objectives: Rewrite an unwritten expectation as an observable work agreement.
Explain how a task connects to its purpose and decision process.
Distinguish a learning question from evidence of poor performance.
lessons.statement: Knowing an acronym is not the same as understanding how the work is done.

image.caption: Clear expectations connect the task, purpose and example.

intro.heading: Make the invisible parts of the job visible
intro.body:
Experienced staff often coordinate through shorthand. They know who reviews a draft, which meeting makes a decision and what “ready to go” means. A new employee may recognize every word and still lack that shared context. If the leader responds with “you will pick it up,” the employee has to learn through avoidable mistakes. Inclusive onboarding makes important expectations visible without treating the colleague as incapable.

Begin with a real task suitable for the role. Explain its purpose, the intended audience, the expected product and the review steps. Provide an example that can be shared under the approved data rules. Point out which features make it useful. A completed memo is more instructive when someone explains why the recommendation is placed first, which evidence supports it and who will use the result.

Unwritten expectations should become workable agreements. “Be proactive” could mean identifying a foreseeable delay early and proposing a next step. “Keep me informed” could mean sending a short update before a review meeting, with decisions and unresolved questions. The leader should explain which expectations are agreed team practices and which are formal agency requirements. Do not let informal preferences quietly become new employment conditions.

Invite questions in a way that makes answering them worthwhile. Ask the colleague to describe their next step, the point where they need a decision and any unclear terms. This checks the instruction, not just the learner. A question about review authority can uncover a missing part of the plan; it should not automatically be read as a lack of judgment.

When a mistake occurs, compare the instruction, available support and task evidence before drawing a broad conclusion. Clarify the expectation and arrange practice appropriate to the role. Actual performance concerns still follow the responsible supervisory and HR process. A learning conversation neither erases those duties nor turns every early question into a personnel judgment.

lessons.keyStatement: A clear expectation names the action, the result and the point where support or a decision is needed.

items.title: “Use good judgment”
items.body: Name a decision the employee can make and one that needs review. Explain the reason for the boundary and provide an example. Judgment develops through context and feedback; it should not mean discovering hidden limits only after crossing them. Keep formal authority and access rules intact.

items.title: “Be collaborative”
items.body: Describe how the team shares drafts, raises disagreements and requests decisions. Avoid evaluating a newcomer mainly by sociability or similarity to the supervisor. Collaboration can be demonstrated through reliable work and respectful exchange in more than one communication style.

items.title: “Ask if you need anything”
items.body: Offer specific occasions and contacts for questions. Some people hesitate when a supervisor appears busy or when they do not know which questions are expected. A scheduled check of the next task can make support practical without requiring constant meetings or dependence.

tabs.label: Purpose
tabs.body: Purpose explains why the task matters and who depends on the result. A newcomer can make better choices when they know that a brief supports a service decision, rather than merely copying the supervisor’s preferred format. This context helps prioritize relevant information while keeping formal instructions and decision authority intact.

tabs.label: Product
tabs.body: A product example makes expectations visible. Explain why its structure, reasoning or evidence is useful, rather than asking for imitation. Use a shareable or practice example so instruction does not expose a real service recipient’s information. The employee can then apply the relevant features to a new task and ask about differences in context.

tabs.label: Boundary
tabs.body: A boundary explains what the employee may decide and what needs review. “Keep everyone informed” can lead either to silence or constant unnecessary updates. Identify the audience, information and decision point. A clear review route allows the newcomer to act with appropriate independence while raising a delay or uncertainty before it affects others.

check.question: A supervisor tells a newcomer to “keep everyone in the loop.” Which clarification is most useful?
check.correct: Identify who needs an update, what information it should contain and when a decision or delay should be raised.
wrong: Tell the employee that experienced people already know what the phrase means.
Ask for updates on every action regardless of relevance.
Rate the employee’s confidence instead of explaining the expectation.
check.feedbackCorrect: This turns a general phrase into an observable agreement linked to the work.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Experienced employees’ familiarity does not make an ambiguous phrase actionable for a newcomer. Reporting every detail burdens both the employee and readers without clarifying purpose. Rating confidence does not establish an update route. Explain who needs which information, when it is useful and when a decision or delay must be raised.

items.text: Raise a likely deadline delay before the scheduled review and propose a next step.
Be more professional in the usual way.
A quiet employee must not care about the team.
Send the person checking the draft a short summary of the decision and outstanding questions.
Handle it like the previous employee did.
An unfamiliar accent means the person lacks policy knowledge.

lessons.next: Next, build connections without making one colleague represent a group.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Jonah is asked to prepare a briefing “like last time.” He has never seen the earlier briefing and does not know the audience. Supervisor Marisol notices his questions and wonders whether he is ready for independent work.
options: Whether Jonah sounds confident enough to proceed without support.
The purpose, shareable example, review steps and missing context in the instruction.
Whether Jonah can persuade a coworker to do the briefing for him.
responses: Confidence does not establish whether the task was explained or whether the work evidence is sound.
This addresses the actual instruction before making a broad judgment about capability.
Support should help Jonah understand and perform the work, not transfer his task to someone else.

lessons.transfer: Rewrite two familiar team phrases as agreements with an action, audience, timing and review boundary. Check whether another reader can explain them.

move.control: You can explain context, give appropriate examples and clarify the decisions within the role.
move.failure: A newcomer is judged against expectations that were never made visible.
move.next: Use the next task check-in to ask what the instruction leaves unclear and revise it accordingly.

lessons.title: Build connections without assigning a cultural role
lessons.summary: Introduce useful relationships while preserving choice, boundaries and the newcomer’s own professional identity.
lessons.objective: Map the work relationships a newcomer needs for one task.
objectives: Map the work relationships a newcomer needs for one task.
Distinguish a practical buddy role from supervision or confidential support.
Identify an introduction that puts an unfair representative burden on an employee.
takeaways: Introduce people through useful work purposes.
Clarify the buddy role and limits.
No newcomer represents an entire community.
lessons.statement: A connection should give someone access to support, not an obligation to explain their identity.

image.caption: Useful introductions explain how colleagues work together.

intro.heading: Make belonging practical and voluntary
intro.body:
A new employee needs more than a list of names. They need to know which relationships help with the work and how to begin a conversation. An introduction to the person who checks drafts may explain the kind of feedback that role offers. A connection with an experienced teammate may help the newcomer find routine information. These introductions make cooperation possible without assuming that people will form the same relationships in the same way.

A buddy arrangement can be helpful when its purpose is specific. The buddy might explain meeting practices, locate routine resources and answer ordinary questions. The supervisor still owns task direction and feedback. HR and other designated offices still handle formal concerns. Do not ask the buddy to keep confidential employment information, approve access or evaluate the newcomer informally on the supervisor’s behalf.

Explain the time commitment and give both people a route to change the arrangement if it is not working. A buddy may be busy, and a newcomer may prefer a different contact for a particular question. Treat that adjustment as a practical improvement rather than disloyalty. Avoid choosing the buddy solely because the two people appear to share an identity; relevant experience and willingness matter.

Introductions should not turn the newcomer into a representative for a cultural group. A statement such as “you can teach us about your community” places an extra role on someone before they have settled into their job. The employee may choose to share an experience, but that choice should not determine their standing. Likewise, an invitation to a voluntary employee group should explain the current group’s purpose and appropriate contact, without assuming membership or assigning diversity work.

Check connections through their usefulness. Does the employee know where to ask about the task, the workplace and formal support? Are important contacts reachable? A full calendar of social meetings does not prove belonging, and a preference for fewer gatherings does not prove isolation.

inThisLesson: Map the relationships needed for work.
lessons.keyStatement: Belonging grows through reliable access and respectful work, not compulsory personal disclosure.

items.title: The buddy becomes an evaluator
items.body: Routine assistance can turn into an informal judgment channel when the supervisor asks for reports about personality or fit. Keep the role clear. Work concerns belong in transparent supervisory processes, not hidden buddy ratings. The newcomer should understand the purpose of each support relationship.

items.title: A shared identity is assumed
items.body: Two people may share a background and still have different interests, experiences or preferences. Ask about willingness and relevant support rather than matching on appearance. Offer more than one useful contact where practical. Do not frame a pairing as proof that every cultural need has been addressed.

items.title: The newcomer is asked to educate everyone
items.body: A voluntary contribution is different from an assumed obligation. Explain the job responsibilities and give the employee genuine choice about optional sharing. Use established learning resources and responsible expertise rather than making one person supply the team’s understanding of a whole community.

tabs.label: Work contact
tabs.body: A work contact has a specific connection to the employee’s responsibilities. Explain what the colleague can help with and when to approach them, rather than arranging many introductions without purpose. A manageable set of relevant contacts helps the newcomer use the network; it does not imply that private familiarity should replace an established approval route.

tabs.label: Routine support
tabs.body: Routine support can help with ordinary questions, vocabulary and where to find information. Clarify what a buddy can do and what remains with the supervisor, HR or another responsible office. A buddy should not become a hidden judge of cultural fit or receive private concerns they are not authorized to handle.

tabs.label: Voluntary connection
tabs.body: Voluntary connection offers current groups and activities with a clear purpose and genuine choice. A person may value these connections without wanting an identity role or cultural presentation. Describe available options and let them choose. Attendance cannot establish commitment or stand in for supervision, and no employee should be introduced as representing every member of a community.

check.question: A supervisor wants to introduce a newcomer by saying they will bring “the perspective of their whole community.” What is the better approach?
check.correct: Introduce the employee’s role and interests they choose to share, without assigning responsibility to represent a community.
wrong: Keep the statement because it sounds complimentary.
Ask the employee to prepare a cultural presentation before doing their assigned work.
Avoid all introductions so no one asks questions.
check.feedbackCorrect: This welcomes the person as a colleague and preserves choice about sharing experience.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A compliment can still assign an unwanted responsibility to represent a whole community. Requiring a cultural presentation adds that burden before the person can focus on their role. Avoiding all introductions loses useful support. Introduce the actual work and interests the employee chooses to share, with relevant contacts and respectful choice.

sorting.heading: Match the relationship to its role

items.text: The person who checks drafts explains when to bring a draft and what feedback they provide.
A buddy is asked to send hidden ratings of the newcomer’s personality.
A newcomer is expected to speak for everyone with their background.
A willing teammate helps locate routine resources.
The buddy is asked to approve the newcomer’s system access.
The employee must deliver the team’s cultural education because of their identity.

lessons.next: Next, design early work that combines contribution and learning.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Noor joins a service team. Supervisor Beth pairs Noor with a colleague based only on a presumed shared background and asks Noor to brief the team about a community. Noor wanted a contact who understands the reporting process.
scenario.prompt: Which change makes the relationship useful?
options: Keep the pairing and cultural briefing because the intentions were welcoming.
Ask about Noor’s work needs, arrange a willing reporting contact and make any personal sharing genuinely optional.
responses: Good intentions do not make the assigned role useful or remove the representative burden.
This removes support instead of improving its purpose and boundaries.
This connects support to the work and gives Noor control over optional personal sharing.

lessons.transfer: Create a relationship map for one practice task. Identify a supervisor, the person who checks the work, routine buddy and formal support route, with a one-sentence purpose for each.

move.control: You can explain roles, ask about willingness and offer connections without making assumptions about identity.
move.failure: The newcomer receives many introductions but no useful work contact, while being assigned extra cultural work.
move.next: Check the purpose and boundaries of the next buddy arrangement with both participants.

lessons.title: Provide early work with usable feedback
lessons.summary: Give a meaningful, manageable task and discuss evidence of the work rather than confidence or similarity.
lessons.objective: Design an early assignment with a clear result and proportionate support.
objectives: Design an early assignment with a clear result and proportionate support.
Write feedback tied to a specific work example and next action.
Identify when a concern belongs in the formal supervisory process.
takeaways: Early work should be meaningful and manageable.
Learning support does not replace formal responsibilities.
lessons.statement: The first task should help a colleague contribute and understand the work, not prove they can succeed without context.

image.caption: Specific feedback helps a new colleague develop usable judgment.

intro.heading: Combine contribution with a chance to learn
intro.body:
A newcomer can be overloaded with high-stakes work or left waiting for something meaningful to do. Both extremes make it difficult to learn the role. A suitable early assignment has a real purpose, a manageable boundary and a way to obtain feedback before an avoidable error affects others. The supervisor should explain why the task is appropriate and what support is available.

Choose a result the employee can understand and complete with the access and information they currently have. For example, a first briefing might examine one defined question rather than an entire program. Explain the audience, expected product, review point and authority limits. Do not give a practice exercise the status of a real service decision, and do not ask an employee to use confidential records they are not authorized to access.

Set a proportionate feedback point. A draft review may be useful before the employee spends hours following an incorrect assumption. Too many approvals, however, can communicate that no judgment is trusted. Ask what uncertainty should be raised early and what choices can be made within the role. Adjust support as the task evidence develops rather than assuming every person needs the same pattern.

Feedback should show its basis. “The summary names the decision clearly; the evidence section needs to distinguish confirmed findings from open questions” is more useful than “you need polish.” Explain the desired revision and invite the employee to describe the reasoning behind the draft. Different work or communication styles can produce a sound result. Examine the actual requirement before treating unfamiliar style as a defect.

If a concern is serious or recurring, use the responsible supervisory and HR process. This course does not create a separate probation rule or informal personnel record. It offers a practical way to make learning support and feedback clearer. Keep real employment documentation in approved channels and use invented examples in these activities.

lessons.keyStatement: Useful feedback connects an observed feature, its effect on the work and a practical revision.

items.title: Too much responsibility too soon
items.body: A real task can still be too broad for the available context. Narrow the question, identify decisions that require review and explain the support. Do not frame a foreseeable failure as a test of toughness. A manageable assignment can reveal judgment more clearly than an unexplained high-stakes request.

items.title: Only low-value busywork
items.body: A newcomer may complete many small tasks without understanding the role’s purpose. Introduce a bounded contribution to actual work when appropriate. Explain its audience and result. Learning does not require immediate independence, but it should connect to meaningful responsibilities rather than filling time.

items.title: Feedback based on familiarity
items.body: A draft that differs from the supervisor’s usual style may still meet the work requirements. Identify the feature that affects clarity, accuracy or usefulness. Explain that connection before requesting a change. Avoid treating confidence, accent or resemblance to a previous employee as evidence of quality.

tabs.label: Observation
tabs.body: Observation names a supported feature of the work. “The brief does not explain why option two was selected” identifies something the employee can examine; “not polished enough” may only express unfamiliar style. Start with the actual requirement so revision is tied to usefulness rather than resemblance to a previous colleague.

tabs.label: Effect
tabs.body: Effect explains what the observed feature changes for the reader or decision. A missing rationale may make it difficult to evaluate the recommendation even when the facts are accurate. Explaining that consequence teaches judgment, rather than requesting a cosmetic rewrite. Check that the claimed effect follows from the task rather than from a supervisor’s personal preference.

tabs.label: Next step
tabs.body: A next step gives the employee a bounded revision and useful review. Ask them to add the comparison rationale, then discuss how they chose the evidence. This keeps them responsible for the work while providing support. Secretly asking a buddy to decide whether they fit the team supplies neither clear feedback nor a fair work expectation.

check.question: A first draft is accurate but unfamiliar in style. What should the supervisor do before requesting revision?
check.correct: Assess it against the task requirements and identify any specific effect on clarity, accuracy or usefulness.
wrong: Reject it because it does not resemble the last employee’s drafts.
Praise confidence instead of reviewing the actual content.
Ask a buddy to secretly decide whether the employee fits the team.
check.feedbackCorrect: The response examines the work’s purpose and evidence rather than resemblance or personality.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Resemblance to the former employee’s drafts is not itself a clarity or accuracy requirement. Praising confidence avoids examining the product. A secret fit judgment by a buddy adds an unsupported personal standard. Review the draft’s purpose and relevant features, explain any effect and agree on a practical revision.

items.text: The recommendation does not identify who must decide.
You just do not have the right feel for this team.
A formal employment concern is routed through the responsible supervisory process.
The draft cites an open question as if it were a confirmed finding.
You need to sound like the previous analyst.
Real performance records stay in approved channels rather than course notes.

lessons.next: Next, review the onboarding experience and improve the process.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Luis prepares a short service briefing. The facts are accurate, but supervisor Dana says it lacks “executive presence.” Dana cannot explain what decision the reader needs or which part of the draft fails to support it.
scenario.prompt: What is the strongest next move?
options: Clarify the briefing’s purpose and identify a specific content or clarity issue before giving a revision request.
Tell Luis to imitate a senior colleague’s personality.
Remove all future meaningful work until Luis appears more confident.
responses: This turns an unclear judgment into feedback tied to the task and an observable revision.
Imitation of personality does not establish whether the work is accurate or useful.
Withholding meaningful work based on confidence does not address the instruction or evidence.

lessons.transfer: Write feedback on a practice draft using one observation, its effect and a next step. Check whether the employee could act without guessing.

move.control: You can choose a bounded assignment, provide examples and give specific feedback through appropriate work channels.
move.failure: The employee learns that sounding familiar matters more than producing accurate, useful work.
move.next: Add a clear purpose and feedback point to the next early assignment.

lessons.title: Review the start and improve what comes next
lessons.summary: Use the employee’s experience and task evidence to improve onboarding without treating every difficulty as a personal deficit.
lessons.objective: Ask a check-in question that identifies an arrangement the supervisor can improve.
objectives: Ask a check-in question that identifies an arrangement the supervisor can improve.
Distinguish a completed activity from evidence that onboarding was useful.
Develop one process change with an owner and a result check.
takeaways: Separate process gaps from individual judgments.
Improve the next start with a clear owner.
lessons.statement: A completed checklist shows activity; a usable start shows that the employee can understand and contribute to the work.

image.caption: A thoughtful check-in examines what helped and what remains unclear.

intro.heading: Learn from the experience without making a diagnosis
intro.body:
An onboarding checklist can be fully marked while a new colleague still lacks a useful contact, clear expectations or workable access. Reviewing the experience means asking what the arrangements enabled and what remained difficult. It is not a search for whether the employee was sufficiently grateful, sociable or resilient. A supervisor should examine the process alongside the task evidence.

Ask concrete questions. Which instruction helped you begin? Where did you have to guess? Which contact was difficult to find? What would have been useful earlier? Explain how the answers will be used and what the supervisor can change. The employee may choose not to share personal experiences; do not treat that choice as a negative signal or promise confidentiality beyond the approved process.

Compare the answers with practical evidence. Was essential access available when needed? Did the first assignment have a clear purpose and review? Were questions answered by an appropriate role? A short anonymous or aggregated review may be useful only when privacy and numbers make it appropriate. In a small team, removing a name does not necessarily prevent identification. Seek responsible data guidance before reporting patterns involving people.

Separate different kinds of issue. A broken link can be corrected in the onboarding material. An unclear role boundary may need a supervisor’s decision. A formal workplace concern needs its designated route. Do not compress these into a single satisfaction score or use a voluntary survey to determine an individual’s intercultural development. These are learning and process questions, not a substitute for formal assessment or employment procedures.

Choose a manageable improvement. Name the arrangement, the change, the owner and a check of whether the next employee can use it. Keep good parts of the experience as well as gaps. A plan that adds more content to every packet may recreate overload. The strongest revision makes a necessary action clearer or support easier to find.

inThisLesson: Assign one improvement and result check.
lessons.keyStatement: Use the experience to improve an arrangement, not to infer a person’s identity, motivation or development stage.

items.title: Every box is checked
items.body: Completion establishes that listed activities were recorded, not that they were understood or useful. Ask about the next task and unresolved questions. Keep required completion records accurate while adding a practical check of readiness. Do not inflate attendance into a claim that all barriers are resolved.

items.title: A small survey looks positive
items.body: A positive response may be informative but cannot establish that everyone had the same experience. Check how many people could respond and whether disclosure felt safe. Avoid reporting identifiable small groups or claiming that silence proves no problem. Describe evidence limits and improve concrete arrangements.

items.title: A concern reaches the wrong channel
items.body: Listen and explain the appropriate route rather than attempting to resolve every issue through onboarding feedback. Formal employment, discrimination, accommodation and safety matters have responsible processes. A process improvement can proceed alongside those processes without replacing them or making an unsupported determination.

tabs.label: Evidence
tabs.body: Evidence distinguishes what occurred from what became usable. Completing orientation sessions establishes attendance; explaining where a draft goes for review establishes a specific piece of work knowledge. Use appropriate minimal information to locate the gap. Do not turn an uncertain answer into an attitude judgment or inferred intercultural assessment.

tabs.label: Change
tabs.body: A change addresses the gap while preserving the responsible process. If the review route is unclear, add its purpose, contact and example at the point the employee first needs it. Check who may authorize the revision. A learning improvement does not remove required instructions or resolve a formal concern through an informal welcome document.

tabs.label: Check
tabs.body: A check tests the next real use rather than assuming the revision worked. Ask a future newcomer to locate the approved review contact when preparing an actual or practice draft. A successful demonstration is stronger evidence than another attendance count. Identify who checks the arrangement and revise it if the same confusion remains.

check.question: An employee attended every session but still does not know where to get a draft reviewed. What does this show?
check.correct: Attendance alone did not establish a usable review route, so the supervisor should clarify and test that arrangement.
wrong: The employee must have an unhelpful attitude toward learning.
The entire onboarding program can be declared successful because attendance is complete.
The employee’s intercultural orientation should be assigned from this answer.
check.feedbackCorrect: The evidence identifies a specific process gap and a practical response without making an unsupported personal judgment.
check.feedbackIncorrect: An attitude label does not explain the missing review contact. Full attendance establishes that sessions occurred, not that the employee can use the route. Inferring an intercultural orientation from one answer is an unsupported personal assessment. Clarify the arrangement and test whether the employee can apply it to the next work task.

items.text: The joining instructions omitted the remote meeting link.
A quiet newcomer cannot collaborate.
Assign a role to confirm the link before the next start.
The employee could not identify who checks the first draft.
No survey comment means every barrier is resolved.
Clarify the review route and check it during the next assignment.

lessons.next: Use the job aid to prepare and review a usable start.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Mei completes orientation and required sessions. At a later check-in, she explains that two team contacts sent her to each other for draft review. Supervisor Arturo sees that the checklist marked “introduced to team” but never named the person who checks drafts.
options: Add several more general orientation sessions.
Name the person who checks drafts and the review steps in the task plan, then confirm a future newcomer can use that route.
Require Mei to repeat orientation because she missed the intended meaning.
responses: More general content may not resolve the specific missing role and could add overload.
This changes the arrangement supported by the evidence and checks its usefulness.
The gap concerns the instruction and role boundary; repetition without clarification shifts responsibility onto Mei.

lessons.transfer: Build a one-page onboarding plan for a colleague. Include preparation, access, expectations, contacts, an early task and one review question with an improvement owner.

move.control: You can review the arrangements, route formal issues and revise a usable plan with responsible colleagues.
move.failure: The checklist becomes proof of success while the employee continues to navigate avoidable uncertainty.
move.next: At the next appropriate check-in, identify one arrangement to improve and confirm its effect during the following start.

jobAid.subtitle: Prepare, explain and review a start that works.
remember: Give the employee a clear next action and useful contact.
Separate formal requirements from voluntary invitations.
Examine arrangements and work evidence without inferring identity or motivation.

sections.heading: Before arrival
items: Confirm joining instructions, essential arrangements and task owners.
Identify fallbacks for delayed equipment or access without bypassing approvals.
Send concise immediate actions and distinguish optional invitations.

sections.heading: Access and expectations
items: Use understandable materials and approved accessibility guidance.
Provide a neutral support route and preserve formal request processes.
Explain the task purpose, product, review steps and authority boundaries.

sections.heading: People and early work
items: Introduce contacts through their work purpose.
Clarify a willing buddy’s role and limits.
Avoid representative burdens and compulsory personal sharing.
Choose a bounded meaningful assignment and a proportionate feedback point.

sections.heading: Review and improve
items: Ask where the employee had to guess and which arrangements helped.
Separate activity completion from evidence of usefulness.
Route formal concerns appropriately and keep personal data in approved channels.
Choose one change, owner and check for the next start.
